entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12539"/><div sID="gen23077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12539"/>3-6. Here follow several questions of a parable-like kind, to awaken conviction in the people.<div eID="gen23077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Can two walk together, except they be agreed?--</hi>Can God's prophets be so unanimous in prophesying against you, if God's Spirit were not joined with them, or if their prophecies were false? The Israelites were "at ease," not believing that God was with the prophets in their denunciations of coming ruin to the nation (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.3">3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.18">1Ki 22:18</reference>, 24, 27; <reference osisRef="Jer.43.2">Jr 43:2</reference>). This accords with <reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Am 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">8</reference>. So "I will be with thy mouth" (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.12">Ex 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.1.8">Jr 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">Mt 10:20</reference>). If the prophets and God were not agreed, the former could not predict the future as they do. In <reference osisRef="Amos.2.12">Am 2:12</reference> He had said, the Israelites forbade the prophets prophesying; therefore, in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.3">Am 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">8</reference>, He asserts the agreement between the prophets and God who spake by them against Israel [Rosenmuller]. Rather, "I once walked with you" (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">Le 26:12</reference>) as a Father and Husband (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>); but now your way and Mine are utterly diverse; there can therefore be no fellowship between us such as there was (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Am 3:2</reference>); I will walk with you only to "punish you"; as a "lion" walks with his "prey" (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Am 3:4</reference>), as a bird-catcher with a bird [Tarnovius]. The prophets, and all servants of God, can have no fellowship with the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.63">Psa 119:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Co 6:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Ep 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.4">Jas 4:4</reference>). <div eID="gen23078" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 3-6. Here follow several questions of a parable-like kind, to awaken conviction in the people. Can two walk together, except they be agreed?-- Can God's prophets be so unanimous in prophesying against you, if God's Spirit were not joined with them, or if their prophecies were false? The Israelites were "at ease," not believing that God was with the prophets in their denunciations of coming ruin to the nation ( Am 6:1 , 3 ; compare 1Ki 22:18 , 24, 27; Jr 43:2 ). This accords with Am 3:7 , 8 . So "I will be with thy mouth" ( Ex 4:12 ; Jr 1:8 ; Mt 10:20 ). If the prophets and God were not agreed, the former could not predict the future as they do. In Am 2:12 He had said, the Israelites forbade the prophets prophesying; therefore, in Am 3:3 , 8 , He asserts the agreement between the prophets and God who spake by them against Israel [Rosenmuller]. Rather, "I once walked with you" ( Le 26:12 ) as a Father and Husband ( Is 54:5 ; Jr 3:14 ); but now your way and Mine are utterly diverse; there can therefore be no fellowship between us such as there was ( Am 3:2 ); I will walk with you only to "punish you"; as a "lion" walks with his "prey" ( Am 3:4 ), as a bird-catcher with a bird [Tarnovius]. The prophets, and all servants of God, can have no fellowship with the ungodly ( Psa 119:63 ; 2Co 6:16 , 17 ; Ep 5:11 ; Jas 4:4 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12543"/><div sID="gen23086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12543"/><hi type="bold">7. his secret--</hi>namely, His purpose hidden from all, until it is revealed to His prophets (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Ge 18:17</reference>). In a wider sense, God's will is revealed to all who love God, which it is not to the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.15">Joh 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.25">17:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen23086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto his servants--</hi>who being servants cannot but obey their Lord in setting forth His purpose (namely, that of judgment against Israel) (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jr 20:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.11">Eze 9:11</reference>). Therefore the fault which the ungodly find with them is groundless (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.17">1Ki 18:17</reference>). It aggravates Israel's sin, that God is not about to inflict judgment, without having fully warned the people, if haply they might repent. <div eID="gen23087" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12548"/><div sID="gen23098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12548"/><hi type="bold">12. shepherd--</hi>a pastoral image, appropriately used by Amos, a shepherd himself.<div eID="gen23098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">piece of ... ear--</hi>brought by the shepherd to the owner of the sheep, so as not to have to pay for the loss (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.39">Ge 31:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.22.13">Ex 22:13</reference>). So if aught of Israel escapes, it shall be a miracle of God's goodness. It shall be but a scanty remnant. There is a kind of goat in the East the ears of which are a foot long, and proportionally broad. Perhaps the reference is to this. Compare on the image <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.34">1Sa 17:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2Ti 4:17</reference>.<div eID="gen23099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that dwell in Samaria in the corner of a bed--</hi>that is, that live luxuriously in Samaria (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">4</reference>). "A bed" means here the Oriental divan, a raised part of the room covered with cushions.<div eID="gen23100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Damascus in a couch--</hi>Jeroboam II had lately restored Damascus to Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.28">28</reference>). So the Israelites are represented as not merely in "the corner of a bed," as in Samaria, but "in a (whole) couch," at Damascus, living in luxurious ease. Of these, now so luxurious, soon but a remnant shall be left by the foe. The destruction of Damascus and that of Samaria shall be conjoined; as here their luxurious lives, and subsequently under Pekah and Rezin their inroads on Judah, were combined (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.1-Isa.8.8">Is 7:1-8; 8</reference>:4, 9; 17:3). The parallelism of "Samaria" to "Damascus," and the Septuagint favor English Version rather than Gesenius: "on a damask couch." The Hebrew pointing, though generally expressing damask, may express the city "Damascus"; and many manuscripts point it so. Compare for Israel's overthrow, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.5">2Ki 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.9-2Kgs.18.12">18:9-12</reference>. <div eID="gen23101" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 12. shepherd-- a pastoral image, appropriately used by Amos, a shepherd himself. piece of ... ear-- brought by the shepherd to the owner of the sheep, so as not to have to pay for the loss ( Ge 31:39 ; Ex 22:13 ). So if aught of Israel escapes, it shall be a miracle of God's goodness. It shall be but a scanty remnant. There is a kind of goat in the East the ears of which are a foot long, and proportionally broad. Perhaps the reference is to this. Compare on the image 1Sa 17:34 , 35 ; 2Ti 4:17 . that dwell in Samaria in the corner of a bed-- that is, that live luxuriously in Samaria (compare Am 6:1 , 4 ). "A bed" means here the Oriental divan, a raised part of the room covered with cushions. in Damascus in a couch-- Jeroboam II had lately restored Damascus to Israel ( 2Ki 14:25 , 28 ). So the Israelites are represented as not merely in "the corner of a bed," as in Samaria, but "in a (whole) couch," at Damascus, living in luxurious ease. Of these, now so luxurious, soon but a remnant shall be left by the foe. The destruction of Damascus and that of Samaria shall be conjoined; as here their luxurious lives, and subsequently under Pekah and Rezin their inroads on Judah, were combined ( Is 7:1-8; 8 :4, 9; 17:3). The parallelism of "Samaria" to "Damascus," and the Septuagint favor English Version rather than Gesenius: "on a damask couch." The Hebrew pointing, though generally expressing damask, may express the city "Damascus"; and many manuscripts point it so. Compare for Israel's overthrow, 2Ki 17:5 , 6 ; 18:9-12 .

The Hebrew pointing, though generally expressing damask, may express the city "Damascus"; and many manuscripts point it so. Compare for Israel's overthrow, 2Ki 17:5 , 6 ; 18:9-12 .
